what_its_for: Glucagon is used to treat very low blood sugar (severe hypoglycemia) in people with diabetes. It works by telling your liver to release stored sugar into your bloodstream, which helps raise your blood sugar back to a safe level quickly. It is used in emergencies when a person is unconscious, having a seizure, or unable to swallow food or juice to treat low blood sugar on their own.
how_to_take: Glucagon comes in different forms depending on the brand. GlucaGen and Gvoke come as an injection given under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a muscle (intramuscular), usually in the outer thigh, upper arm, or buttock. Baqsimi is a nasal powder that is sprayed into one nostril — you do not need to inhale or breathe it in. Because this medicine is for emergencies, a family member, caregiver, or friend should know how to use it BEFORE an emergency happens. Read the instructions that come with your kit carefully and ask your pharmacist or doctor to show you and your caregiver how to use it. After giving glucagon, call 911 (emergency services) right away. Turn the person on their side to prevent choking. Once the person wakes up and is able to swallow, give them a fast-acting sugar snack such as juice or glucose tablets, followed by a longer-acting snack like crackers with peanut butter.
dosing: Adults and children weighing 55 pounds (25 kg) or more: The usual dose is 1 mg. Children weighing less than 55 pounds (25 kg): The usual dose is 0.5 mg. Baqsimi nasal powder: One 3 mg spray into one nostril for all ages. If the person does not respond within 15 minutes, a second dose may be given if another kit is available while waiting for emergency help. Always follow the specific instructions that come with your glucagon kit, as directions may vary slightly between brands.
missed_dose: Glucagon is only used in emergencies and is not taken on a regular daily schedule, so there is no missed dose to worry about. Keep your glucagon kit with you or nearby at all times so it is ready if you need it. Check the expiration date regularly and replace it before it expires.
storage: Store glucagon at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C) or as directed on the package. Do not freeze glucagon and do not store it in direct sunlight or in a hot car. Keep it in its original kit or case until you are ready to use it. Once mixed (for kits that require mixing), use it right away — do not save it for later. Check the expiration date on your kit regularly and get a new kit before it expires. Keep out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Do not use glucagon if the solution looks cloudy, discolored, or contains particles (for injectable forms). Do not use it past the expiration date. Do not inject glucagon into a vein (intravenous). Avoid storing glucagon in extreme heat, cold, or humidity such as a bathroom medicine cabinet. Do not delay calling 911 after using glucagon — it is a temporary treatment and the person needs medical attention even if they feel better.
when_to_call_doctor: Call 911 (emergency services) immediately after giving glucagon. Contact your doctor as soon as possible after any episode of severe low blood sugar to find out why it happened and how to prevent it in the future. Call your doctor or seek emergency help if the person does not wake up or respond within 15 minutes after receiving glucagon, if they vomit and cannot keep food or sugar down after waking up, if low blood sugar episodes are happening more often, or if you have questions about how to use your glucagon kit properly.
when_it_works: Glucagon usually starts working within 5 to 15 minutes after injection or nasal spray. Most people will begin to wake up or regain consciousness within this time. Once awake and able to swallow, give the person a snack containing sugar to help keep blood sugar levels stable. Full recovery may take up to 30 minutes or longer depending on the severity of the low blood sugar episode.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Glucagon may be used during pregnancy or while breastfeeding in a life-threatening emergency. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits. Older adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to the effects of glucagon. Use with care and follow your doctor's instructions. Children: Glucagon can be used in children — the dose is based on the child's weight. Make sure caregivers and school staff know how to use it. Kidney or liver disease: Glucagon may not work as well in people with severe liver disease because the liver needs to function properly to release stored sugar. Tell your doctor if you have liver problems.
